lessons.title: Bloom filter: maybe vs definitely not
lessons.why_here: You'll meet it in front of slow lookups: RocksDB and Cassandra check one per on-disk table file before reading it, and caches use them to skip misses.
lessons.tldr: A Bloom filter answers membership with 'definitely not' or 'maybe': no false negatives, some false positives.
lessons.intuition: Picture a row of switches, all off. To add a word, run it through three hash functions (each turns the word into a switch number) and flip those switches on. To ask about a word, check its three switches. One off means it was never added. All on might be its own switches, or ones other words flipped.
lessons.explanation:
A filter has `m` bits and `k` hash functions. Adding an item sets its `k` bits; a lookup reads the same `k` bits. Bits only go from 0 to 1, so an added item's bits stay set: one 0 proves the item is absent. All 1s is only **maybe**, because other items may have set those bits.

With `n` items the false-positive rate is about (1 − e^(−kn/m))^k. Ten bits per item with `k` = 7 gives about 0.8%, whatever the size of the items.

- Use it to skip expensive lookups that usually miss, then confirm each maybe against the real data.
- You can't delete: clearing a bit could erase other items. Counting Bloom filters use counters instead of bits to allow it.
- Overfill it and nearly every answer becomes maybe.
lessons.in_this_change: RocksDB keeps a Bloom filter per SST file when one is configured (its default filter policy is none), Cassandra one per SSTable by default. A read checks each file's filter and skips the files that say definitely not, so a key that isn't there usually costs no data-block reads. A false positive costs a wasted read, never a wrong result.

figure.title: Three questions, one bit array
figure.caption: Hog hits a 0, so definitely not. Lark hits only 1s set by others. Type a word, or add it.

takeaways: A 0 bit proves absence; all 1s only means maybe.
The fuller the bit array, the more false positives.

quiz.question: The filter holds cat, dog and fox. Two of hog's three bits are 1 and one is 0. What does a lookup for hog answer?
quiz.explanation: A 0 bit can only mean hog was never added, since adding sets every one of its bits. Two 1s don't count toward anything; they were set by other words.

quiz.question: You keep `m` and `k` fixed and add twice as many items. What changes?
choices: False positives get more likely; false negatives stay impossible
Nothing, since the rate depends only on k
The oldest items' bits get cleared to make room
quiz.explanation: More items set more bits, so an absent item more often finds all its bits set. Bits are never cleared, so an added item can't come back definitely not.
